claim: Children, adolescents, and adults (ages 8–27 years, N = 122) completed an adapted version of a recently developed value-guided decision-making task that decouples novelty and uncertainty.
source: Here, children, adolescents, and adults (ages 8–27 years, N = 122) completed an adapted version of a recently developed value-guided decision-making task that decouples novelty and uncertainty.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample characteristics and task completion.

claim: Exploration decreased with increasing age.
source: In line with prior studies, we found that exploration decreased with increasing age.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Participants of all ages demonstrated a similar bias to select choice options with greater novelty.
source: Critically, participants of all ages demonstrated a similar bias to select choice options with greater novelty, whereas aversion to reward uncertainty increased into adulthood.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Aversion to reward uncertainty increased into adulthood.
source: Critically, participants of all ages demonstrated a similar bias to select choice options with greater novelty, whereas aversion to reward uncertainty increased into adulthood.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Adolescents and adults demonstrated attenuated uncertainty aversion for more novel choice options.
source: Computational modeling of participant choices revealed that whereas adolescents and adults demonstrated attenuated uncertainty aversion for more novel choice options, children's choices were not influenced by reward uncertainty.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling of the study data.

claim: Children's choices were not influenced by reward uncertainty.
source: Computational modeling of participant choices revealed that whereas adolescents and adults demonstrated attenuated uncertainty aversion for more novel choice options, children's choices were not influenced by reward uncertainty.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling of the study data.

claim: Children tend to know less about the world and have longer temporal horizons over which to exploit newly discovered information relative to adults.
source: Relative to adults, children tend to know less about the world and have longer temporal horizons over which to exploit newly discovered information (Gopnik, 2020; Gopnik et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It may be advantageous to explore to a greater extent earlier in life, and gradually shift to a more exploitative decision strategy as experience yields knowledge.
source: Thus, it may be advantageous to explore to a greater extent earlier in life, and gradually shift to a more exploitative decision strategy as experience yields knowledge.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on the preceding discussion about children's knowledge and temporal horizons.

claim: Children and adolescents tend to explore more than adults.
source: Children and adolescents tend to explore more than adults (Christakou et al., 2013; Giron et al., 2022; Jepma et al., 2020; Lloyd et al., 2021; Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019; Schulz et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Increased exploration promotes enhanced learning about the structure of the environment.
source: and this increased exploration promotes enhanced learning about the structure of the environment (Blanco and Sloutsky, 2021; Liquin and Gopnik, 2022; Sumner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Across development, stimulus novelty influences exploration.
source: Prior work has revealed that across development, two features of choice options influence exploration: stimulus novelty (Daffner et al., 1998; Gottlieb et al., 2013; Henderson and Moore, 1980; Jaegle et al., 2019; Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Wittmann et al., 2008) and reward uncertainty (Badre et al., 2012; Blanco and Sloutsky, 2021; Gershman, 2018; Somerville et al., 2017; Trudel et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Across development, reward uncertainty influences exploration.
source: Prior work has revealed that across development, two features of choice options influence exploration: stimulus novelty (Daffner et al., 1998; Gottlieb et al., 2013; Henderson and Moore, 1980; Jaegle et al., 2019; Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Wittmann et al., 2008) and reward uncertainty (Badre et al., 2012; Blanco and Sloutsky, 2021; Gershman, 2018; Somerville et al., 2017; Trudel et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Novelty refers to the extent to which choice options have been previously encountered.
source: Here, we use novelty to refer to the extent to which choice options have been previously encountered and uncertainty to refer to the variance in the distributions of rewards that they yield.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided by the authors.

claim: Uncertainty refers to the variance in the distributions of rewards that choice options yield.
source: Here, we use novelty to refer to the extent to which choice options have been previously encountered and uncertainty to refer to the variance in the distributions of rewards that they yield.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided by the authors.

claim: Adults were novelty-seeking, preferentially selecting choice options that they had encountered infrequently in the past versus those that were more familiar.
source: Adults were novelty-seeking, preferentially selecting choice options that they had encountered infrequently in the past versus those that were more familiar.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a prior study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Adults were uncertainty averse, such that they tended to avoid options with high reward uncertainty.
source: However, adults were also uncertainty averse, such that they tended to avoid options with high reward uncertainty.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a prior study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Stimulus novelty diminished the influence of uncertainty on exploratory choice in adults.
source: Computational modeling further revealed that stimulus novelty diminished the influence of uncertainty on exploratory choice.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling findings from a prior study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: The influences of novelty and uncertainty have not been disentangled in children and adolescents.
source: To date, however, the influences of novelty and uncertainty have not been disentangled in children and adolescents.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: On trials in which the two choice options had similar expected values, participants selected the more novel option on 58.7% of trials.
source: On trials in which the two choice options had similar-expected-values (<0.05 difference), participants selected the more novel option on 58.7% (SE = 0.8%) of trials and the more uncertain option on only 46.2% (SE = 0.9%) of trials.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: On trials in which the two choice options had similar expected values, participants selected the more uncertain option on only 46.2% of trials.
source: On trials in which the two choice options had similar-expected-values (<0.05 difference), participants selected the more novel option on 58.7% (SE = 0.8%) of trials and the more uncertain option on only 46.2% (SE = 0.9%) of trials.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Children's choices were significantly influenced by expected value.
source: Results indicated that children's choices were significantly influenced by both expected value (OR = 2.27 [1.78, 2.91], χ2(1) = 26.8, p < 0.001) and novelty (OR = 1.35 [1.24, 1.48], χ2(1) = 28.4, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of children's data.

claim: Children's choices were significantly influenced by novelty.
source: Results indicated that children's choices were significantly influenced by both expected value (OR = 2.27 [1.78, 2.91], χ2(1) = 26.8, p < 0.001) and novelty (OR = 1.35 [1.24, 1.48], χ2(1) = 28.4, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of children's data.

claim: There was not an effect of uncertainty on children's choice.
source: However, there was not an effect of uncertainty on choice, OR = 1.07 [0.945, 1.21], χ2(1) = 1.17, p = 0.280, indicating no significant evidence for uncertainty-seeking.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of children's data.

claim: Children selected the more novel option on 59.1% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: Corroborating these findings, on trials in which the two choice options had nearly identical expected values (<0.05 difference), children, adolescents, and adults, on average, selected the more novel option on 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), and 58.3% (SE = 1.2%) of trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Adolescents selected the more novel option on 59.1% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: Corroborating these findings, on trials in which the two choice options had nearly identical expected values (<0.05 difference), children, adolescents, and adults, on average, selected the more novel option on 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), and 58.3% (SE = 1.2%) of trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Adults selected the more novel option on 58.3% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: Corroborating these findings, on trials in which the two choice options had nearly identical expected values (<0.05 difference), children, adolescents, and adults, on average, selected the more novel option on 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), 59.1% (SE = 1.7%), and 58.3% (SE = 1.2%) of trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Adults selected the more uncertain option on only 41.9% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: However, whereas adults tended to avoid the more uncertain option, selecting it on only 41.9% (SE = 1.2%) of equal-expected-value trials, adolescents and children selected the more uncertain option on 48.9% (SE = 1.7%) and 52.7% (SE = 1.7%) of these trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Adolescents selected the more uncertain option on 48.9% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: However, whereas adults tended to avoid the more uncertain option, selecting it on only 41.9% (SE = 1.2%) of equal-expected-value trials, adolescents and children selected the more uncertain option on 48.9% (SE = 1.7%) and 52.7% (SE = 1.7%) of these trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Children selected the more uncertain option on 52.7% of equal-expected-value trials.
source: However, whereas adults tended to avoid the more uncertain option, selecting it on only 41.9% (SE = 1.2%) of equal-expected-value trials, adolescents and children selected the more uncertain option on 48.9% (SE = 1.7%) and 52.7% (SE = 1.7%) of these trials, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Age-related decreases in exploratory choices were driven by an increase in aversion to reward uncertainty with increasing age.
source: Thus, taken together, these results suggest that age-related decreases in exploratory choices were driven by an increase in aversion to reward uncertainty with increasing age.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results across age groups.

claim: Participants responded more quickly when selecting options with higher expected values.
source: Participants responded more quickly when selecting options with higher expected values (b = −0.03, SE = 0.006, F(1, 115.4) = 29.7, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of response time data.

claim: Participants responded more slowly when selecting options with higher novelty.
source: and more slowly when selecting options with higher novelty (b = 0.06, SE = 0.004, F(1, 111.3) = 197, p < 0.001) and higher uncertainty (b = 0.07, SE = 0.005, F(1, 117.1) = 171.7, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of response time data.

claim: Participants responded more slowly when selecting options with higher uncertainty.
source: and more slowly when selecting options with higher novelty (b = 0.06, SE = 0.004, F(1, 111.3) = 197, p < 0.001) and higher uncertainty (b = 0.07, SE = 0.005, F(1, 117.1) = 171.7, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of response time data.

claim: Novelty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of younger versus older participants.
source: Novelty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of younger versus older participants, whereas uncertainty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of older versus younger participants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of response time data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Uncertainty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of older versus younger participants.
source: Novelty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of younger versus older participants, whereas uncertainty had a stronger slowing influence on the response times of older versus younger participants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of response time data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Children's response times were sensitive to the uncertainty of the selected option.
source: Critically, however, we continued to observe a significant effect of uncertainty on response times when we only included children's data in the model, b = 0.04, SE = 0.01, F(1, 38.2) = 16.5, p < 0.001, indicating that children's response times were sensitive to the uncertainty of the selected option
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of children's response time data.

claim: Despite not demonstrating uncertainty aversion in their decisions, children were sensitive to the relative reward uncertainty of different choice options throughout the task.
source: Thus, taken together, our findings suggest that despite not demonstrating uncertainty aversion in their decisions, children were sensitive to the relative reward uncertainty of different choice options throughout the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the response time findings in children.

claim: Adult choices were best characterized by a model in which choice utilities took into account interactions between novelty and uncertainty.
source: In line with findings from Cockburn et al., 2022, we found that adult choices were best characterized by a model in which choice utilities took into account interactions between novelty and uncertainty.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling of adult data.

claim: Adult choices were best captured by the familiarity-gated uncertainty model.
source: Specifically, adult choices were best captured by the familiarity-gated uncertainty model (PXP Familiarity Gate = 1), in which uncertainty aversion was greater for more familiar options.
evidence: This is a finding from computational model comparison for adults.

claim: Adolescent choices were best captured by the familiarity-gated uncertainty model.
source: Despite showing weaker aversion to uncertainty relative to adults, adolescents were also best fit by this model (PXP Familiarity Gate = 1).
evidence: This is a finding from computational model comparison for adolescents.

claim: Children's choices were best captured by a model with a simple novelty bias.
source: Children's choices, however, were best captured by a model with a simple novelty bias (PXP Novelty Bias = 0.62; PXP Familiarity Gate = 0.38).
evidence: This is a finding from computational model comparison for children.

claim: Children optimistically initiated the value of novel options.
source: Children's average 'novelty bias' (from the group-level novelty bias model fits) was 1.49, indicating that they optimistically initiated the value of novel options.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling parameter estimates for children.

claim: Children's novelty bias was significantly different from 0.
source: A one-sample hierarchical Bayesian inference (HBI) t-test examining the group-level posterior distribution of the novelty bias parameter (implemented via the cbm model-fitting package Piray et al., 2019), revealed that children's novelty bias was significantly different from 0, t(16.3) = 5.96, p < 0.001.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical testing of model parameters.

claim: The average value of the uncertainty bias was −0.15 for both adolescents and adults.
source: The average value of the 'uncertainty bias' (from the group-level familiarity-gated uncertainty model fits) was −0.15 for both adolescents and adults.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling parameter estimates.

claim: Uncertainty bias parameter estimates were significantly different from 0 in both adolescents and adults.
source: HBI t-tests revealed that uncertainty bias parameter estimates were significantly different from 0 in both age groups (Adolescents: t(26.5) = −7.8, p < 0.001; Adults: t(11.3) = −4.16, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical testing of model parameters.

claim: Adults and adolescents were more strongly deterred by the uncertainty of familiar options versus novel ones.
source: Thus, these modeling results suggest that whereas adults and adolescents were more strongly deterred by the uncertainty of familiar options versus novel ones, children employed a simpler learning algorithm in which they optimistically initialized the value of novel choice options.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: Children employed a simpler learning algorithm in which they optimistically initialized the value of novel choice options.
source: Thus, these modeling results suggest that whereas adults and adolescents were more strongly deterred by the uncertainty of familiar options versus novel ones, children employed a simpler learning algorithm in which they optimistically initialized the value of novel choice options.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: Children's bias toward exploration over exploitation may arise from attenuated aversion to selecting more uncertain options rather than heightened sensitivity to novelty.
source: These findings suggest that children's bias toward exploration over exploitation may arise from attenuated aversion to selecting more uncertain options rather than heightened sensitivity to novelty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: Novelty may be intrinsically rewarding.
source: Prior studies have found that novelty may be intrinsically rewarding (Wittmann et al., 2008), motivating individuals to approach, learn about, and remember the new stimuli they encounter (Houillon et al., 2013; Krebs et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
source: Children (Henderson and Moore, 1980; Mendel, 1965; Valenti, 1985), adolescents (Spear, 2000), and adults (Cockburn et al., 2022; Daffner et al., 1998) all demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adolescents demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
source: Children (Henderson and Moore, 1980; Mendel, 1965; Valenti, 1985), adolescents (Spear, 2000), and adults (Cockburn et al., 2022; Daffner et al., 1998) all demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adults demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
source: Children (Henderson and Moore, 1980; Mendel, 1965; Valenti, 1985), adolescents (Spear, 2000), and adults (Cockburn et al., 2022; Daffner et al., 1998) all demonstrate novelty-seeking behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The drive to engage with novel stimuli promotes exploratory choice in a consistent manner across the age range studied.
source: Indeed, our findings suggest that the drive to engage with novel stimuli promotes exploratory choice in a consistent manner across our age range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Differences in the reward value assigned to novel options cannot fully account for developmental differences in exploration.
source: Moreover, the consistency of novelty-seeking across development indicates that differences in the reward value assigned to novel options cannot fully account for developmental differences in exploration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of novelty-seeking across age.

claim: Individuals across age demonstrate uncertainty aversion in some environments.
source: Prior studies of decision making have found that individuals across age demonstrate uncertainty aversion in some environments (Camerer and Weber, 1992; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Rosenbaum and Hartley, 2019) and uncertainty-seeking in others (Blanchard and Gershman, 2018; Giron et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals across age demonstrate uncertainty-seeking in some environments.
source: Prior studies of decision making have found that individuals across age demonstrate uncertainty aversion in some environments (Camerer and Weber, 1992; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Rosenbaum and Hartley, 2019) and uncertainty-seeking in others (Blanchard and Gershman, 2018; Giron et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In environments where learned information can be exploited to improve subsequent choices, resolving uncertainty has high utility.
source: In environments where learned information can be exploited to improve subsequent choices, resolving uncertainty has high utility (Rich and Gureckis, 2018; Wilson et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In choice contexts with short temporal horizons, there is little opportunity to use learned reward information to improve future decisions.
source: whereas in choice contexts with short temporal horizons, there is little opportunity to use learned reward information to improve future decisions (Camerer and Weber, 1992; Levy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children's reduced uncertainty aversion may have emerged from insensitivity to the limited utility of gaining additional information about the most uncertain choice options.
source: In our task, individuals had a relatively short horizon over which to exploit reward probabilities that themselves required multiple trials to learn — children's reduced uncertainty aversion may have emerged from insensitivity to the limited utility of gaining additional information about the most uncertain choice options (Somerville et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, with a citation to related work.

claim: The developmental decrease in uncertainty-seeking behavior observed in this study is in line with what has been observed in prior studies in which uncertainty was easier to discern.
source: Indeed, the developmental decrease in uncertainty-seeking behavior that we observed here is in line with what has been observed in prior studies in which uncertainty was easier to discern.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior research.

claim: In one study, children tended to select choice options with hidden reward amounts over those with visible reward amounts.
source: For example, in one study (Blanco and Sloutsky, 2021), children tended to select choice options with hidden reward amounts over those with visible reward amounts.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a cited prior study.

claim: Young children often use experiences of surprise or the coherence of their own beliefs about the world to direct their exploration toward uncertain parts of the environment.
source: In studies of causal learning and exploratory play, young children often use experiences of surprise or the coherence of their own beliefs about the world to direct their exploration toward uncertain parts of the environment (Bonawitz et al., 2012; Schulz and Bonawitz, 2007; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children are sensitive to uncertainty even when it depends on distributions of binary outcomes.
source: Here, we extend these past findings to demonstrate that children are sensitive to uncertainty even when it depends on distributions of binary outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings in relation to prior work.

claim: By adulthood, novelty and uncertainty interact competitively, exerting opposing motivational influences on decision-making.
source: Our computational modeling findings largely replicated previous work suggesting that by adulthood, novelty and uncertainty interact competitively (Cockburn et al., 2022), exerting opposing motivational influences on decision-making.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results, with reference to prior work.

claim: Activation in the ventral striatum reflects a biased reward prediction error consistent with optimistic value initialization for novel stimuli in adults.
source: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), this prior adult study (Cockburn et al., 2022) revealed that activation in the ventral striatum reflects a biased reward prediction error consistent with optimistic value initialization for novel stimuli, whereas activation in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) reflects the subjective utility of uncertainty reduction.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a cited prior fMRI study.

claim: Activation in the medial prefrontal cortex reflects the subjective utility of uncertainty reduction in adults.
source: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), this prior adult study (Cockburn et al., 2022) revealed that activation in the ventral striatum reflects a biased reward prediction error consistent with optimistic value initialization for novel stimuli, whereas activation in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) reflects the subjective utility of uncertainty reduction.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a cited prior fMRI study.

claim: The integration of uncertainty into mPFC value representations was diminished for novel stimuli in adults.
source: In line with choices being best characterized by a model in which the aversive influence of uncertainty was dampened by novelty, the integration of uncertainty into these mPFC value representations was similarly diminished for novel stimuli (Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on findings from a cited prior fMRI study.

claim: Attenuated uncertainty aversion for novel stimuli may promote exploration even in environments where deriving the prospective utility of uncertainty reduction is difficult.
source: Cockburn et al., 2022 posited that attenuated uncertainty aversion for novel stimuli may promote exploration even in environments where deriving the prospective utility of uncertainty reduction is difficult.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from a cited prior study.

claim: Competitive interactions between uncertainty and novelty may emerge in adolescence, as connectivity between cortical and subcortical circuitry matures.
source: Our findings further suggest that these competitive interactions between uncertainty and novelty may emerge in adolescence, as connectivity between cortical and subcortical circuitry matures (Casey et al., 2019; Parr et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, with citations to related work on brain development.

claim: Heightened exploration is an adaptive quality of childhood.
source: Recent theories have proposed that heightened exploration is an adaptive quality of childhood (Giron et al., 2022; Gopnik, 2020)
evidence: This claim is based on recent theoretical proposals cited in the text.

claim: The developmental shift from more exploratory to more exploitative behavior may arise from strengthening aversion to selecting options with higher reward uncertainty with increasing age.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the developmental shift from more exploratory to more exploitative behavior may arise from strengthening aversion to selecting options with higher reward uncertainty with increasing age, rather than from changes in novelty-seeking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results in the study.

claim: One hundred and twenty-two participants between the ages of 8 and 27 years old completed the experiment.
source: One hundred and twenty-two participants between the ages of 8 and 27 years old (mean age = 17.9 years, SD age = 5.6 years, 62 females, 59 males, 1 non-binary) completed the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The final analyzed sample comprised n = 30 children, n = 30 adolescents, and n = 62 adults.
source: The final analyzed sample of 122 participants comprised n = 30 children (mean age = 10.5 years; SD age = 1.4 years; range = 8.1–12.7 years; 14 females), n = 30 adolescents (mean age = 15.5 years; SD age = 1.3 years; range = 13.6–17.8 years; 16 females), and n = 62 adults (mean age = 22.6 years; SD age = 2.8 years; range = 18.1–27.8 years; 32 females).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample broken down by age group.

claim: The task was divided into 10 blocks of 15 trials.
source: The task was divided into 10 blocks of 15 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task structure.

claim: Half of the blocks were 'easy' with reward probabilities of 80%, 50%, and 20%.
source: Half of the blocks were 'easy' — in easy blocks, the creature's favorite hiding spot held a coin on 80% of trials, their second favorite held a coin on 50% of trials, and their least favorite held a coin on 20% of trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task design.

claim: Half of the blocks were 'hard' with reward probabilities of 70%, 50%, and 30%.
source: The other half of blocks were 'hard' — in hard blocks, the creature's favorite hiding spot held a coin on 70% of trials, their second favorite held a coin on 50% of trials, and their least favorite held a coin on 30% of trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task design.

claim: After the first block, each subsequent block contained two hiding spots that participants had encountered in previous blocks and one novel hiding spot.
source: Importantly, after the first block, each subsequent block contained two hiding spots that participants had encountered in previous blocks and one novel hiding spot they had not seen before.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task design.

claim: The reward probabilities were re-randomized for every creature.
source: Though participants had already encountered two of the hiding spots within each block, the reward probabilities were re-randomized for every creature.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task design.

claim: Participants demonstrated above-chance memory for the most rewarding choice within each block.
source: Participants also demonstrated above-chance (defined as 0.2) memory for the most rewarding choice within each block (mean = 0.25; standard error [SE] = 0.001; t(119) = 4.02, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of memory test data.
